title: Consonance and Dissonance
intro: Some intervals sound stable and smooth (consonant), others tense or rough (dissonant). Part of the difference is acoustic and part is musical convention, and the two have shifted over the centuries.

items: Perfect consonances: unison, octave, perfect fifth (and, between upper voices, the perfect fourth).
Imperfect consonances: major and minor thirds and sixths.
Dissonances: seconds, sevenths, the tritone and every augmented or diminished interval. In two-voice counterpoint and over the bass, the perfect fourth is treated as a dissonance too.

blocks.text: In tonal music a dissonance is expected to resolve: one of its notes moves by step to a consonance. That pull is what drives harmony forward. A dominant seventh chord contains a tritone (B–F in G7), and its resolution (B up to C, F down to E) is the core of the V–I cadence.

Two pure tones close in frequency beat: their sum swells and fades |f₁ − f₂| times per second. Slow beating (a few per second) sounds like a wavering; around 20–30 beats per second it becomes a harsh roughness; when the tones are far enough apart (beyond the ear's critical band) the roughness disappears and we hear two separate pitches.

Plomp and Levelt (1965) measured how rough two sine tones sound as their spacing changes: roughness peaks at about a quarter of a critical band and fades by about a whole one. Real instrument tones have many partials, and the roughness of an interval is the sum over every pair of partials. Sethares (1993) fitted a formula to their curve; summing it gives the dissonance curve below.

widget.title: Sensory dissonance of two harmonic tones

blocks.text: With one partial (pure sine tones) the curve has a single hump just above the unison and is smooth everywhere else: sine tones have no 'consonant intervals'. Add partials and dips appear exactly where partials of the two tones coincide: the octave (1200), the fifth (702), the fourth (498), the major sixth (884), the major third (386) and the minor third (316). The deepest dips are at the simplest ratios. The tritone (600) and the seconds and sevenths sit on high ground.

This is why consonance depends on timbre. Sethares showed that tones with stretched, inharmonic partials (like bells or synthesised spectra) have their dips in different places, and that scales sound best when their intervals match the dips of the instrument's own spectrum.

Acoustics does not explain everything. The perfect fourth is acoustically smooth yet was treated as a dissonance over the bass in common-practice music. The major third was considered dissonant in early medieval music (in Pythagorean tuning it is a rough 81:64) and became the most characteristic consonance of the Renaissance once tuning made it pure. In jazz, sevenths and ninths are part of the normal sonority and need no resolution. Consonance is partly what the style teaches the listener to expect.

widget.title: Consonance to dissonance, played as harmonic intervals

blocks.text: Play a minor second low on the keyboard (C2–D♭2) and then high (C6–D♭6). The low one is muddy and harsh; the high one merely sparkles. Low in the range the critical band is wide compared with the notes' spacing, so even thirds sound thick. This is why pianists voice chords with wide intervals (octaves and fifths) in the left hand and keep close thirds above about C3.

blocks.title: Beats
blocks.text: A piano tuner plays A4 = 440 Hz against a string at 437 Hz. How many beats per second does she hear, and which way must the string go?
solution: Beat rate = |440 − 437| = 3 beats per second. The string is flat, so it must be tightened (raised) until the beats stop.

blocks.title: Coinciding partials
blocks.text: Why does a just major third (5:4) sound smoother than an equal-tempered one (400 cents)?
solution: In 5:4 the lower tone's 5th partial and the upper tone's 4th partial coincide exactly (both 5f). In equal temperament the third is 13.7 cents wider, so those partials are slightly apart and beat. At middle C the 5th partial is about 1308 Hz, and 13.7 cents there is about 10 Hz, so the third beats roughly 10 times a second.
blocks.answer: Its 5th and 4th partials coincide; tempered, they beat about 10 times a second near middle C
